nameStory: The name 'puffin' likely comes from the bird's distinctly round, puffed-out appearance, especially when viewed head-on. These charismatic seabirds have also earned the nickname 'sea parrots' due to their colorful, oversized beaks that resemble a parrot's bill. The 'Atlantic' part simply distinguishes them from their Pacific cousins, the tufted and horned puffins.
description: Atlantic puffins are stocky, penguin-like seabirds with a distinctive upright stance on land and comical appearance that makes them instant crowd-pleasers. They sport crisp black and white plumage like a formal tuxedo, but their most striking feature is an enormous, triangular beak painted in bold orange, red, and black stripes during breeding season. These accomplished swimmers spend most of their lives at sea, only coming to shore to nest on rocky coastal cliffs and islands. Adults typically measure about the size of a small duck, with males being slightly larger than females.

idTips.label: Colorful triangular beak
idTips.description: The massive, flattened beak is unmistakable during breeding season - bright orange at the base with red and black markings, feeling hard and ridged if you could touch it. In winter, the beak becomes smaller and duller grayish-brown.

idTips.label: Tuxedo plumage
idTips.description: Crisp black cap and back contrast sharply with bright white chest and belly, like a perfectly pressed formal outfit. The feathers feel dense and waterproof, designed for ocean life.

idTips.label: Orange webbed feet
idTips.description: Bright orange legs and large webbed feet that would feel leathery and surprisingly strong. These paddle-like feet are perfect for swimming underwater and gripping rocky cliff faces.

idTips.label: Light gray cheek patches
idTips.description: Pale gray facial discs on either side of the head, like soft powder puffs against the black cap. These patches help distinguish adults from juveniles, which have darker gray cheeks.

idTips.label: Stocky, upright posture
idTips.description: On land, stands bolt upright like a tiny penguin, with a compact, barrel-shaped body that rocks slightly when walking. This distinctive stance makes them unmistakable even from a distance.

habitat: In New England, Atlantic puffins are found only along the Maine coast, particularly on offshore islands like Eastern Egg Rock and Machias Seal Island. They nest in burrows they dig into the grassy tops of rocky sea cliffs and isolated islands, preferring areas with soft soil for excavation. During non-breeding season, they live entirely at sea in the cold waters of the North Atlantic.

seasonality.spring: Puffins return to Maine's coastal islands in late spring to begin breeding, showing off their full colorful beak displays and bright orange feet. This is the best time to see them on land at nesting colonies.
seasonality.summer: Peak viewing season as adults tend to eggs and chicks in cliff-top burrows, frequently flying back and forth from sea with beaks stuffed full of small fish. Their colors are at their most vibrant during this breeding period.
seasonality.fall: Puffins begin leaving their nesting islands and head back to open ocean, with their bright beak colors starting to fade as they molt into winter plumage.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England shores, spending the season far out at sea with much duller, smaller beaks and overall more subdued appearance until spring returns.

funFact: Puffins are underwater flying machines - they literally 'fly' through the water using their wings as propellers, reaching speeds up to 55 mph while chasing fish 200 feet below the surface, making them some of the most athletic birds on Earth.
confusionNotes: In winter plumage, puffins might be confused with other black-and-white seabirds like murres or razorbills, but puffins always have that distinctive stocky, round body shape and upright posture. Remember: 'Puffins are pudgy, murres are lean' - even without the colorful beak, their roly-poly build gives them away.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that puffins are actually more closely related to auks and murres than to penguins, despite their similar appearance and upright stance. The resemblance is due to convergent evolution - both groups evolved similar body plans for life in cold ocean waters, but penguins are Southern Hemisphere birds while puffins rule the North Atlantic.
compareHints: Atlantic puffins are the only puffin species you'll see in New England waters, as their closest relatives are the tufted and horned puffins of the Pacific Ocean. Within the auk family, puffins are distinguished from murres and razorbills by their much more colorful beaks, rounder body shape, and distinctive light gray cheek patches rather than pure white faces.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its Atlantic cousin that New Englanders might know, the Tufted Puffin has those signature golden head plumes and a completely black back and underparts during breeding season.
